\chapter{Introducing Yourself}
\label{ch:introductions}
\hlchaptermodality{2}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can introduce myself in Kannada, give my name, and understand the other person's name.}

Run the whole introduction: give your name, ask for theirs, and close with santōṣa — then name the one Sanskrit word in it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hesaru]{\kn{ಹೆಸರು} (hesaru) — \textquotedblleft{}name,\textquotedblright{} and the \emph{p}$\to$\emph{h} shift}

\label{lesson:KA-C02-hesaru}



\begin{quote}
\textquotedblleft{}Name\textquotedblright{} — and a word that shows off a famous Kannada sound-law.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Kannada.)} \textbf{\kn{ಹ}} (ha) + \textbf{\kn{ೆ}} (the \emph{e}-sign) $\to$ \textbf{\kn{ಹೆ}} (he); \textbf{\kn{ಸ}} (sa); \textbf{\kn{ರು}} (ru). Read \textbf{\kn{ಹೆ}·\kn{ಸ}·\kn{ರು}} $\to$ \textbf{hesaru}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಹೆಸರು}} (\emph{hesaru}, \textquotedblleft{}name\textquotedblright{}) is \textbf{native Dravidian}, from Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*pesar} — and it hides a famous Kannada sound-law: an old initial \emph{p} became \emph{h}. So \textbf{*pesar $\to$ *hesar $\to$ hesaru}. That makes it a \textbf{cousin of Tamil \emph{peyar}} (same root; Tamil kept the \emph{p}, Kannada softened it to \emph{h}) — and, like \emph{peyar}, \emph{not} related to Sanskrit \emph{nāma} (Hindi \emph{nām}, English \emph{name}).

Across the family: Kannada \emph{hesaru}, Tamil \emph{peyar}, Telugu \emph{pēru}, Malayalam \emph{pēr} — one Dravidian word; only Hindi \emph{nām} / English \emph{name} are Indo-European.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=violet!6,colframe=violet!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Across the family — the same idea, five ways}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Language} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Name\textquotedblright{}} & \textbf{Source} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Kannada} & \kn{ಹೆಸರು} \emph{hesaru} & Dravidian *pesar (p$\to$h) \\
Tamil & \emph{peyar} & the \emph{same} Dravidian root (kept \emph{p}) \\
Telugu & \emph{pēru} & the \emph{same} Dravidian root \\
Malayalam & \emph{pēr} & the \emph{same} Dravidian root \\
Hindi & \emph{nām} & Sanskrit (Indo-European) \\
English & \emph{name} & Indo-European \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The \emph{p}$\to$\emph{h} shift is why \emph{hesaru} looks unlike its sisters — but it is the same word.
\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hesaru\textquotedblright{}
  \item the shift — \emph{*pesar} $\to$ \emph{hesaru} (p $\to$ h)
  \item its Tamil cousin — \emph{peyar}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What sound-law turned \emph{*pesar} into \emph{hesaru}, and what Tamil word is its cousin? (\emph{p} $\to$ \emph{h}; Tamil \emph{peyar}.) Is it related to English \emph{name}? (No — native Dravidian.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nanna]{\kn{ನನ್ನ} (nanna) — \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:KA-C02-nanna}



\begin{quote}
\textquotedblleft{}My\textquotedblright{} — native Dravidian, with no European cousin.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Kannada.)} \textbf{\kn{ನ}} (na) + the conjunct \textbf{\kn{ನ್ನ}} (nna) $\to$ \textbf{nanna} — a doubled, held \emph{nn}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ನನ್ನ}} (\emph{nanna}) means \textquotedblleft{}my.\textquotedblright{} It belongs to Kannada's native Dravidian first-person family, not to the Indo-European family behind English \emph{I/my}. The stem underneath is Dravidian *nān — the same one behind Tamil \emph{nāṉ} / \emph{eṉ}. You will meet the related word for \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} in its own lesson; today you only need \emph{nanna}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nanna\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{nanna} once with its meaning, \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\kn{ನನ್ನ}} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}My.\textquotedblright{}) Is it native Dravidian or an Indo-European loan? (Native Dravidian.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nanna hesaru …]{\kn{ನನ್ನ} \kn{ಹೆಸರು} … (nanna hesaru …) — \textquotedblleft{}my name is…,\textquotedblright{} with no \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:KA-C02-nanna-hesaru}



\begin{quote}
Assemble the two atoms — and notice, as in Tamil, no word for \textquotedblleft{}is.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The phrase, assembled}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item nanna (my) + hesaru (name) + your name.
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ನನ್ನ} \kn{ಹೆಸರು} …} = \textquotedblleft{}my name …\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}my name is…\textquotedblright{}}
\end{quote}

\emph{Nanna hesaru Arun.} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}My name is Arun.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the zero copula}]
There is \textbf{no verb}. Kannada sets \textquotedblleft{}my name\textquotedblright{} beside \textquotedblleft{}Arun\textquotedblright{} and lets the \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} be understood — the \textbf{zero copula} of the Dravidian family (just like Tamil). \emph{Nanna hesaru Arun} = literally \textquotedblleft{}my name Arun.\textquotedblright{}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nanna hesaru …\textquotedblright{} with your name
  \item notice — no word for \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give your name in Kannada. (\emph{Nanna hesaru ….}) What does Kannada leave out that English needs? (The verb \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} — zero copula.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nīnu / nīvu]{\kn{ನೀನು} / \kn{ನೀವು} (nīnu / nīvu) — \textquotedblleft{}you,\textquotedblright{} familiar and respectful}

\label{lesson:KA-C02-niinu-niivu}



\begin{quote}
\textquotedblleft{}You\textquotedblright{} — and Kannada makes respect the same way Tamil and French do.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Kannada.)} \textbf{\kn{ನೀ}} (nī) + \textbf{\kn{ನು}} (nu) $\to$ \emph{nīnu}; \textbf{\kn{ನೀ}} + \textbf{\kn{ವು}} (vu) $\to$ \emph{nīvu}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ನೀನು}} (\emph{nīnu}, familiar \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*nīn} — the same native root as Tamil \emph{nī}. \textbf{\kn{ನೀವು}} (\emph{nīvu}) is the respectful/plural \textquotedblleft{}you.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: respect by the plural}]
\emph{nīnu} (familiar) vs. \emph{nīvu} (respectful, and literally plural) — the same politeness-by-plural as Tamil \emph{nīṅgaḷ} and French \emph{vous}: one respected person addressed as \textquotedblleft{}you all.\textquotedblright{} For a first meeting, \textbf{nīvu}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}nīnu\textquotedblright{} (familiar), \textquotedblleft{}nīvu\textquotedblright{} (respectful)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Kannada make \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} respectful, and which languages use the same trick? (By the plural — \emph{nīvu}; Tamil \emph{nīṅgaḷ}, French \emph{vous}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ēnu]{\kn{ಏನು} (ēnu) — \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:KA-C02-enu}



\begin{quote}
The last piece of the question: \textquotedblleft{}what.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Kannada.)} \textbf{\kn{ಏ}} (independent long \emph{ē}, word-initial) + \textbf{\kn{ನು}} (nu) $\to$ \textbf{ēnu}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಏನು}} (\emph{ēnu}, \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}) is native Dravidian, on the interrogative stem \textbf{*yā- / *e-} — the same Dravidian question-root as Tamil \emph{eṉṉa}, heading Kannada's question family: \emph{ēnu} (what), \emph{yāru} (who), \emph{elli} (where), \emph{yāke} (why).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ēnu\textquotedblright{}
  \item the question family — ēnu, yāru, elli
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Dravidian stem heads \textbf{\kn{ಏನು}} and Kannada's other question-words? (\emph{*yā-/*e-}, the same as Tamil \emph{eṉṉa}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nimma hesaru ēnu?]{\kn{ನಿಮ್ಮ} \kn{ಹೆಸರು} \kn{ಏನು}? (nimma hesaru ēnu?) — \textquotedblleft{}what's your name?\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:KA-C02-nimma-hesaru-enu}



\begin{quote}
Assemble the question — your + name + what — still no \textquotedblleft{}is.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The phrase, assembled}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ನಿಮ್ಮ}} (\emph{nimma}, \textquotedblleft{}your\textquotedblright{}) = the possessive of \emph{nīvu} (\textquotedblleft{}you,\textquotedblright{} respectful).
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ನಿಮ್ಮ} \kn{ಹೆಸರು} \kn{ಏನು}?} = literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{your name what?}\textquotedblright{} = \textquotedblleft{}what's your name?\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Three words, \textbf{no verb} — the zero copula holds for questions too.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: answer, and the familiar version}]
Answer with the sentence you built: \textbf{Nanna hesaru Arun.} The familiar \textquotedblleft{}your\textquotedblright{} is \emph{ninna} (from \emph{nīnu}): \emph{ninna hesaru ēnu?}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nimma hesaru ēnu?\textquotedblright{}
  \item ask, then answer — \textquotedblleft{}nimma hesaru ēnu?\textquotedblright{} / \textquotedblleft{}nanna hesaru …\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\kn{ನಿಮ್ಮ} \kn{ಹೆಸರು} \kn{ಏನು}?} literally say, and what's missing vs. English? (\textquotedblleft{}Your name what?\textquotedblright{}; no \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} — zero copula.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[e]{\kn{◌ೆ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:KA-S111-vowel-sign-e}



\begin{quote}
One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{◌ೆ}}
\textbf{\kn{◌ೆ}} — \emph{e}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it with \emph{e}. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

You already say these, and every one of them has \kn{◌ೆ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಹೆಸರು}} \emph{hesaru} — name
  \item \textbf{\kn{ನಿಮ್ಮ} \kn{ಹೆಸರು} \kn{ಏನು}?} \emph{nimma hesaru ēnu?} — what is your name?
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{◌ೆ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \kn{◌ೆ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \kn{◌ೆ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ಹೆಸರು}  ·  \kn{ಹೌದು}  ·  \kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{◌ೆ} three times, saying \emph{e} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \kn{◌ೆ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{◌ೆ}? What vowel does it put on the consonant it attaches to — and what does it take off? (\textbf{Puts \emph{e} on; takes the built-in \emph{a} off.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[santōṣa]{\kn{ಸಂತೋಷ} (santōṣa) — \textquotedblleft{}joy,\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}pleased to meet you\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:KA-C02-santosha}



\begin{quote}
The warm close — and, true to Kannada, a Sanskrit word where Tamil used a native one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The phrase}
The full form is \textbf{\kn{ನಿಮ್ಮನ್ನು} \kn{ಭೇಟಿಯಾಗಿ} \kn{ಸಂತೋಷ}} (\emph{nimmannu bhēṭiyāgi santōṣa}) — \textquotedblleft{}having met you, joy.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಸಂತೋಷ}} (\emph{santōṣa}, \textquotedblleft{}joy, contentment\textquotedblright{}) is \textbf{Sanskrit} — \emph{sam-} (\textquotedblleft{}fully\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{toṣa} (\textquotedblleft{}satisfaction\textquotedblright{}) — not native. Where Tamil reaches for its home-grown \emph{magiḻcci}, Kannada uses a Sanskrit word even for \textquotedblleft{}pleased.\textquotedblright{} The same split you saw over \textquotedblleft{}hello\textquotedblright{} (\emph{namaskāra}) and \textquotedblleft{}thanks\textquotedblright{} (\emph{dhanyavāda}) runs right through the introductions: Kannada borrows, Tamil keeps its own.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}santōṣa\textquotedblright{}
  \item the split — Kannada \emph{santōṣa} (Sanskrit) vs. Tamil \emph{magiḻcci} (native)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \textbf{\kn{ಸಂತೋಷ}} native or borrowed, and what does the contrast with Tamil show? (Sanskrit; Kannada borrows Sanskrit — here for \textquotedblleft{}pleased\textquotedblright{} — where Tamil keeps native \emph{magiḻcci}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[u]{\kn{◌ು} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:KA-S02-vowel-sign-u}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{ನ} — what does it do?

\textbf{\kn{◌ು}} — \emph{u}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it with \emph{u}. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

  \item \textbf{\kn{ಏನು}} \emph{ēnu} — what
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{◌ು} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \kn{◌ು} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\section[Practice]{Chapter 2 — the introduction, whole}

\label{lesson:KA-C02-practice}



\begin{quote}
Every atom built. Here's the exchange.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The dialogue}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Kannada} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\kn{ನನ್ನ} \kn{ಹೆಸರು} \kn{ಮೀರಾ}. (\emph{nanna hesaru Mira}) & My name is Mira. \\
\kn{ನಿಮ್ಮ} \kn{ಹೆಸರು} \kn{ಏನು}? (\emph{nimma hesaru ēnu}) & What's your name? \\
\kn{ನನ್ನ} \kn{ಹೆಸರು} \kn{ಅರುಣ್}. (\emph{nanna hesaru Arun}) & My name is Arun. \\
\kn{ಸಂತೋಷ}. (\emph{santōṣa}) & Pleased to meet you. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Every atom traced:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{hesaru} $\leftarrow$ Dravidian \emph{*pesar} (p$\to$h; cousin of Tamil \emph{peyar}, \emph{not} \emph{name})
  \item \textbf{nanna} $\leftarrow$ \emph{nānu} (\textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{ēnu} $\leftarrow$ Dravidian question-stem \emph{*yā-/*e-}
  \item \textbf{santōṣa} $\leftarrow$ \textbf{Sanskrit} (Kannada borrows even for \textquotedblleft{}pleased\textquotedblright{}; Tamil keeps native \emph{magiḻcci})
\end{itemize}

The Kannada habit: the \textbf{zero copula} (no \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}). And the family thread — native Dravidian grammar words, a Sanskrit word for \textquotedblleft{}pleased.\textquotedblright{}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the whole exchange, both voices
  \item your own introduction — \textquotedblleft{}nanna hesaru …\textquotedblright{}
  \item ask it back — \textquotedblleft{}nimma hesaru ēnu?\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give your name, ask someone else's, say you're pleased. (\emph{Nanna hesaru …. / Nimma hesaru ēnu? / Santōṣa.}) Which word here is Sanskrit, not native? (\emph{santōṣa} — \textquotedblleft{}pleased.\textquotedblright{})

Next chapter: \emph{hēgiddīra?} (\textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{}) and answering with \emph{chennāgiddēne} — the responding cycle.
\end{tcolorbox}
